title: Conversions, Ratios and Dosage Basics
objective: Convert between common units and use ratio-proportion to solve basic dosage and intake problems.
body:
Health care math is about accuracy: a misplaced decimal can cause harm.

**Metric conversions.** 1 kilogram (kg) = 1,000 grams (g); 1 g = 1,000 milligrams (mg); 1 mg = 1,000 micrograms (mcg); 1 liter (L) = 1,000 milliliters (mL). Moving to a smaller unit, multiply; moving to a larger unit, divide.

**Household and weight.** 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb; 1 teaspoon (tsp) = 5 mL; 1 tablespoon (Tbsp) = 15 mL; 1 fluid ounce (oz) = 30 mL; 1 inch = 2.54 cm.

**Temperature.** °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9 and °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32.

**Ratio and proportion.** Set up known ratio = unknown ratio and cross-multiply. Example: an order is 250 mg; tablets are 125 mg each. 125 mg/1 tab = 250 mg/x tabs, so x = 2 tablets.

**Formula method.** Dose = (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity. Desired 500 mg, have 250 mg per 5 mL: (500 ÷ 250) × 5 = 10 mL.

**Military time.** 1:00 p.m. = 1300; 11:45 p.m. = 2345; midnight = 0000.

Always label units in every step and double-check that the answer is reasonable.
examples: 8 oz of water = 8 × 30 = 240 mL of intake.

questions.stem: How many milligrams are in 2.5 grams?
A patient weighs 176 lb. What is the weight in kilograms?
The order is 500 mg. Tablets contain 250 mg each. How many tablets?
How many milliliters are in 2 tablespoons?
What is 9:30 p.m. in military time?
Desired dose 300 mg; available 150 mg per 5 mL. How many mL?
A patient drinks 6 fl oz of juice. What is the intake in mL?
